opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't arrive at it from the top down. Early on, like a lot of people in this field, we started with the technology. We had strong models, we had decent hardware, and the instinct was: let's build a general robot and then go find where it fits. That turned out to be backwards.

What changed things for me was spending a lot of time on-site. Factories, warehouses, a few commercial kitchens. I'd stand next to a line worker for a whole shift and just watch. And what you notice is that the hard part is almost never the "impressive" part. It's not the single dramatic grasp you'd put in a demo video. It's the long tail: the box that's slightly crushed, the bag that's half-open, the part that came in rotated ninety degrees, the moment when something falls and the person just casually fixes it without thinking. Humans absorb thousands of these small exceptions every day, and nobody writes them down because to them it's not even a task.

So the problem we needed to solve gradually became clear: it wasn't "can the robot do the task," it was "can the robot keep doing the task for eight hours when the world keeps being slightly wrong." Reliability under messiness. That reframed everything: what data we collected, how we thought about recovery behaviors, even how we talked to customers. A customer doesn't care that you hit ninety-five percent success in the lab. If one in twenty attempts needs a human to walk over, you haven't removed labor, you've just moved it.

The second thing I learned was about the economics. The people actually buying these systems think in terms of throughput, uptime, and how many headcount-hours they can redeploy. If you can't translate your capability into that language, it doesn't matter how elegant the model is. So understanding the problem meant understanding their spreadsheet as much as their workflow.

And the third, which took me longest to accept: you have to pick a narrow enough entry point to actually get deployed, get real data back, and let that flywheel start turning. The generality comes later, earned through deployment, not designed in up front. That was a bit of a humbling realization, because the ambition in this field is always "general-purpose." But the path there, I think, runs through being genuinely useful somewhere specific first.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes learning from on-site observation, customer economics, and narrow deployment entry points, but does not mention conversations with PhD students, their advisors, or expanding into a wider expert network.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it didn't come from a whiteboard. It came from standing in a factory in Dongguan for three weeks and watching people work.

When we started, we had the typical engineer's assumption: build a general-purpose robot arm with good perception, and the use cases will reveal themselves. So we went to potential customers with a demo. The demo was impressive. Nobody bought it.

What changed my understanding was one shift supervisor. He walked me to a station where a worker was picking cables out of a bin and plugging them into connectors. Thousands of times a day. The cables were tangled, the lighting changed from morning to afternoon, and every batch from the supplier looked slightly different. He said, "If you can do this one thing reliably, I'll buy ten. If you can do a hundred things at ninety percent, I don't want any."

That reframed everything for us. The problem wasn't intelligence in the abstract. The problem was reliability under messy, changing conditions, on tasks that were boring, repetitive, and increasingly impossible to hire for. Young people simply don't want these jobs anymore, and the factory owners feel that every single month.

So we stopped asking "what can the robot do" and started asking "what does this line lose money on when a person doesn't show up." That meant spending far more time on data from real sites than on lab benchmarks. It meant our failure modes had to degrade gracefully, because a robot that stops the line is worse than no robot at all. And it meant the product had to be deployable by the factory's own technicians, not by a team of our PhDs flying in.

I'd say the deepest lesson was humility. The customers understood their problems far better than we did. Our job was to listen long enough to hear which problem was actually worth solving first.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the team identified the problem through factory visits, observing workers, and listening to a shift supervisor. It does not describe expanding conversations from PhD students through their advisors into a wider expert network.

astra-6.text:
For me, the starting point is the task, rather than the robot. What is someone trying to get done? Where do they struggle today? And would putting intelligence into a physical machine actually help?

That distinction matters because a compelling demonstration and a useful product are quite different things. In a demonstration, you can control the environment. In actual use, objects move, conditions change, and people do things you didn’t anticipate. So the problem isn’t simply whether the robot can perform an action. It’s whether it can do it reliably enough that someone can depend on it—and recover when something goes wrong.

That’s how I think about understanding the product: identify a concrete need, test the smallest useful task, and let the failures show you what you still haven’t understood.

r001.rationale: The response discusses identifying concrete user needs and testing tasks, but it does not describe expanding conversations from PhD students to their advisors and a wider expert network.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the starting point was understanding where embodied intelligence could be useful in practice. What is someone trying to accomplish, what makes that difficult today, and what would a robot actually need to do to help?

That changes how you define the problem. A demonstration might show that a robot can perform a task once. A useful product has to perform it reliably, handle variation, and recover when something goes wrong. It also has to fit into the way people already work.

So I think the key is to keep bringing the technical questions back to the user’s task. The problem you need to solve is not simply how to make the robot more capable. It’s which capability will make a meaningful difference, and whether you can deliver it consistently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical user needs and reliable robot performance, but does not describe expanding conversations from PhD students and their advisors into a wider expert network.
